questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.image_title: Histopathology of skin biopsy showing suprabasal acantholysis
key_findings: Acantholytic cells floating in blister cavity
questions.question_text: A 45-year-old woman presents with painful oral erosions for 3 months followed by flaccid blisters on trunk and extremities. The blisters rupture easily leaving raw erosions. Nikolsky sign is positive. A skin biopsy is shown. Which of the following immunofluorescence findings would confirm the diagnosis?

options.A: Linear IgG and C3 at the dermoepidermal junction
options.B: IgG deposition in a 'fishnet/chicken wire' pattern throughout the epidermis
options.C: IgA deposits at the tips of dermal papillae
options.D: C3 deposits at the BMZ in a granular pattern

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Pemphigus vulgaris shows IgG anti-desmoglein 3 (and/or 1) antibodies depositing in intercellular spaces giving a 'fishnet/chicken wire' pattern on direct immunofluorescence. Histology shows suprabasal acantholysis with tombstone appearance of basal cells. Incorrect (A): Linear IgG and C3 at DEJ is seen in Bullous Pemphigoid (subepidermal blistering, tense blisters, negative Nikolsky). Incorrect (C): IgA at dermal papillae tips is characteristic of Dermatitis Herpetiformis (associated with gluten sensitivity, intensely pruritic). Incorrect (D): Granular C3 at BMZ is seen in Lupus band test (SLE). EXAM PEARL: Pemphigus = Painful, Pemphigoid = Pruritic. Desmoglein 3 (mucosa) + Desmoglein 1 (skin) in PV. Treatment: high-dose steroids + rituximab/azathioprine.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A 38-year-old man with a 10-year history of plaque psoriasis presents with pain and swelling of the distal interphalangeal joints of fingers, sausage-shaped swelling of the right index finger, and pitting of nails. X-ray shows 'pencil-in-cup' deformity. What is the most appropriate first-line systemic therapy for his joint disease?

options.A: Hydroxychloroquine
options.B: Methotrexate
options.C: Colchicine
options.D: Leflunomide alone

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Methotrexate is the first-line DMARD for psoriatic arthritis (PsA), particularly when skin and joint disease coexist. It addresses both components. Incorrect (A): Hydroxychloroquine can worsen psoriasis and is contraindicated in PsA. Incorrect (C): Colchicine is used for gout, not PsA. Incorrect (D): Leflunomide has evidence in PsA but is not preferred first-line over methotrexate. EXAM PEARL: PsA patterns - DIP involvement, dactylitis (sausage digit), enthesitis, and axial disease. 'Pencil-in-cup' deformity = arthritis mutilans (severe form). If MTX fails → anti-TNF agents (etanercept, adalimumab) or IL-17 inhibitors (secukinumab).

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A 32-year-old farmer from rural Bihar presents with a 6-month history of multiple hypopigmented anesthetic patches over the trunk and extremities. Slit-skin smear shows a Bacteriological Index (BI) of 4+. He is started on MDT. After 3 weeks, he develops sudden worsening of existing lesions with new erythematous plaques, fever, and severe neuritis with risk of motor paralysis. What is the MOST appropriate immediate management?

options.A: Stop MDT immediately and start dapsone monotherapy
options.B: Continue MDT and add high-dose prednisolone; consider clofazimine increase
options.C: Stop MDT and administer thalidomide 400mg/day
options.D: Continue MDT, add NSAIDs, and observe for 2 weeks

questions.explanation: Correct (B): This is Type 1 lepra reaction (Reversal Reaction) presenting with acute neuritis and worsening skin lesions. It is a medical emergency due to risk of permanent nerve damage. Management = Continue MDT (NEVER stop) + high-dose prednisolone (40-60mg/day, taper over 3-6 months). Clofazimine dose may be increased to 300mg/day for anti-inflammatory effect. Incorrect (A): MDT must never be stopped during lepra reactions - it may worsen the bacterial load. Incorrect (C): Thalidomide is used for Type 2 (ENL) reactions, NOT Type 1. In Type 1, thalidomide is ineffective. Incorrect (D): NSAIDs alone are insufficient for neuritis; delay in steroid therapy can cause irreversible nerve damage. EXAM PEARL: Type 1 (Reversal) = BT/BB/BL leprosy = CMI upregulation = treat with steroids. Type 2 (ENL) = LL/BL = immune complex = treat with thalidomide or steroids. Dapsone + Rifampicin + Clofazimine = MB MDT for 12 months.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.image_title: Trichoscopy showing yellow dots, black dots and exclamation mark hairs
key_findings: Yellow dots (follicular infundibulum filled with sebum)
questions.question_text: A 19-year-old woman presents with a 2-month history of a well-defined circular patch of hair loss on the scalp with no scarring. Trichoscopy findings are shown. She also mentions nail pitting. Which statement about her condition is MOST accurate?

options.A: It is caused by scarring inflammation of hair follicles
options.B: It is mediated by T-cell attack on the hair follicle bulb and has 5% lifetime risk of alopecia totalis
options.C: Dermoscopy showing black dots and exclamation mark hairs are diagnostic
options.D: First-line treatment is oral finasteride

questions.explanation: Correct (C): Trichoscopy (dermoscopy of scalp) in alopecia areata characteristically shows yellow dots, black dots, exclamation mark hairs, and short vellus hairs. These findings together are diagnostic of AA. Incorrect (A): AA is non-scarring alopecia - follicular openings are preserved. Scarring alopecias include lichen planopilaris, discoid lupus, etc. Incorrect (B): Partially true - it is T-cell mediated (CD8+ lymphocytes attack follicular bulb). But the lifetime risk of progression to alopecia totalis/universalis is approximately 5-10%, not uniformly high. This option is misleading. Incorrect (D): Finasteride is used for androgenetic alopecia (male/female pattern hair loss). First-line for localized AA = intralesional triamcinolone acetonide. EXAM PEARL: AA associations - atopy, autoimmune thyroid disease, Down syndrome, vitiligo. 'Swarm of bees' pattern on histology = peribulbar lymphocytic infiltrate.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A 28-year-old man presents with generalized lymphadenopathy, diffuse maculopapular rash involving palms and soles, and mucous patches in the mouth. He reports a painless genital ulcer that healed spontaneously 6 weeks ago. RPR is reactive at 1:64. FTA-ABS is positive. He is allergic to penicillin. What is the best alternative treatment?

options.A: Azithromycin 1g single dose
options.B: Doxycycline 100mg twice daily for 14 days
options.C: Ceftriaxone 1g IM daily for 10 days
options.D: Erythromycin 500mg four times daily for 14 days

questions.explanation: Correct (B): This patient has secondary syphilis (rash on palms/soles, mucous patches, lymphadenopathy following primary chancre). First-line = Benzathine Penicillin G 2.4 MU IM single dose. In penicillin allergy: Doxycycline 100mg BD x 14 days is the recommended alternative for non-pregnant patients with early syphilis. Incorrect (A): Azithromycin has been used but macrolide resistance (A2058G mutation in T. pallidum) is increasing globally; not currently recommended by most guidelines. Incorrect (C): Ceftriaxone has some evidence but is not the standard recommended alternative and data is limited. Incorrect (D): Erythromycin is less reliable due to poor CNS penetration and variable efficacy; not preferred. EXAM PEARL: Secondary syphilis = 'The Great Imitator'. Palm/sole rash + condyloma lata + mucous patches. VDRL/RPR = screening (non-treponemal, titre correlates with disease activity). FTA-ABS = confirmatory (treponemal, remains positive for life).

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A 6-year-old child with atopic dermatitis is brought by his mother who reports his eczema is not responding to moderate-potency topical steroids applied for 3 weeks. Examination shows widespread eczematous plaques with numerous vesicles, crusting, and satellite lesions. Tzanck smear from a vesicle shows multinucleated giant cells. The most appropriate management is:

options.A: Increase topical steroid potency to very high and add topical calcineurin inhibitor
options.B: Systemic acyclovir and continue moisturizers; withhold topical steroids temporarily
options.C: Systemic antibiotics for secondary bacterial infection
options.D: Start dupilumab immediately

questions.explanation: Correct (B): The clinical picture describes Eczema Herpeticum (Kaposi's varicelliform eruption) - HSV superinfection on atopic skin. Multinucleated giant cells on Tzanck smear confirms herpetic infection. Treatment = systemic acyclovir (IV in severe/disseminated cases, oral if mild). Topical steroids should be temporarily withheld as they can worsen viral spread. Moisturizers are continued. Incorrect (A): Increasing steroids in eczema herpeticum is dangerous - steroids suppress immune response and worsen HSV spread, potentially causing fatal dissemination. Incorrect (C): Although secondary bacterial infection (often S. aureus) can co-exist, the primary pathogen here is HSV (confirmed by Tzanck smear), and antiviral is the priority treatment. Incorrect (D): Dupilumab (IL-4/IL-13 inhibitor) is used for moderate-severe AD refractory to conventional treatment - not in acute herpetic infection. EXAM PEARL: Eczema herpeticum = emergency. Punched-out erosions + fever + rapid spread in atopic patient = think HSV. Risk factors = severe AD, filaggrin mutations.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A 22-year-old student presents with multiple hypo- and hyperpigmented macules on the trunk, more prominent after sun exposure. KOH mount of skin scrapings shows 'spaghetti and meatballs' appearance. Which organism is responsible and what is the most effective treatment for widespread disease?

options.A: Trichophyton rubrum; oral terbinafine for 2 weeks
options.B: Malassezia furfur; oral itraconazole 200mg/day for 5-7 days
options.C: Candida albicans; topical clotrimazole for 4 weeks
options.D: Epidermophyton floccosum; selenium sulfide shampoo

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Tinea versicolor (pityriasis versicolor) is caused by Malassezia furfur (now M. globosa). KOH shows short hyphae + round spores = 'spaghetti and meatballs'. For widespread disease, oral itraconazole 200mg/day for 5-7 days (or fluconazole 400mg single dose) is most effective. Incorrect (A): Trichophyton rubrum causes tinea pedis, cruris, corporis, unguium - not tinea versicolor. Terbinafine has poor activity against Malassezia. Incorrect (C): Candida causes oral thrush, vaginal candidiasis, intertrigo - not the 'spaghetti and meatballs' picture. Incorrect (D): Epidermophyton floccosum causes tinea pedis/cruris. Selenium sulfide is used topically for tinea versicolor but is not the 'most effective' for widespread disease. EXAM PEARL: Malassezia is a lipophilic yeast - normal skin flora that becomes pathogenic. Hypopigmentation due to azelaic acid production (inhibits tyrosinase). Does NOT fluoresce on Wood's lamp reliably (may show faint yellow-green). KOH is diagnostic.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: An 18-year-old female student presents with painful nodules and cysts predominantly on the jawline and chin, with several comedones. She reports worsening before her menstrual cycle. She has tried multiple topical treatments without success. She is currently not on contraception. What is the MOST appropriate next step in management?

options.A: Prescribe oral isotretinoin immediately
options.B: Prescribe oral doxycycline 100mg BD + topical adapalene/benzoyl peroxide
options.C: Prescribe combined oral contraceptive pill (COCP) with anti-androgen activity
options.D: Refer for intralesional steroid injections only

questions.explanation: Correct (B): This patient has moderate-severe nodulocystic acne with hormonal pattern (jawline, premenstrual flare). Before initiating isotretinoin (requires pregnancy test, iPLEDGE enrollment, teratogenicity counseling) or hormonal therapy, a course of oral antibiotic (doxycycline) + topical combination (adapalene + BPO) is appropriate as next step after topical therapy failure. Incorrect (A): Isotretinoin is indicated for severe/recalcitrant nodulocystic acne. However, in a female not on contraception, the mandatory iPLEDGE protocol (2 forms of contraception, monthly pregnancy tests) must be initiated first - it cannot be started 'immediately' without these safeguards. Incorrect (C): COCP (e.g., cyproterone acetate/ethinyl estradiol) is effective for hormonal acne but requires evaluation for contraindications (thromboembolism risk) and patient preference. It is not the MOST appropriate next step before antibiotic trial. Incorrect (D): Intralesional triamcinolone is useful for individual large cysts but not definitive treatment. EXAM PEARL: Acne treatment ladder: Topical retinoid/BPO → Oral antibiotic + topical → Hormonal (females) → Oral isotretinoin. Isotretinoin: teratogenic (Category X), causes xerosis, elevated LFTs, depression (controversial), decreased night vision.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A 25-year-old woman with extensive vitiligo involving >30% BSA presents requesting treatment. She has tried topical steroids and topical tacrolimus without adequate response. She is otherwise healthy. Which of the following represents the MOST appropriate next-line therapy with best evidence for repigmentation in extensive vitiligo?

options.A: Excimer laser (308nm) to all affected areas
options.B: Narrowband UVB (NB-UVB) phototherapy
options.C: Oral minipulse dexamethasone (OMP) and PUVA combination
options.D: Afamelanotide implant alone

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Narrowband UVB (311nm) is the gold standard for extensive vitiligo (>10-15% BSA). It is safe, effective, suitable for all ages including children, and can be used during pregnancy. Given >30% BSA involvement, NB-UVB is the treatment of choice. Incorrect (A): Excimer laser (308nm) is highly effective for localized/focal vitiligo but is impractical for extensive disease due to time constraints and cost per session. Incorrect (C): PUVA (psoralen + UVA) is less preferred than NB-UVB due to higher side effects (phototoxicity, ocular toxicity, carcinogenesis). OMP (oral minipulse dexamethasone) is used to arrest progression (active/spreading vitiligo) rather than induce repigmentation in stable extensive disease. Incorrect (D): Afamelanotide (α-MSH analogue) is used as adjuvant to NB-UVB for faster repigmentation, not as monotherapy. EXAM PEARL: NB-UVB = preferred for generalized vitiligo. Excimer laser = preferred for localized stable vitiligo. Surgical options (suction blister grafting, melanocyte transplant) = stable vitiligo. New treatments: ruxolitinib (JAK inhibitor) cream - FDA approved 2022 for non-segmental vitiligo.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A 35-year-old HIV-positive man who was started on nevirapine 3 weeks ago presents with high fever, painful skin blistering, and detachment of epidermis involving 45% of body surface area. Oral, ocular, and genital mucosae are all involved. SCORTEN score is calculated as 4. Which of the following management strategies has the BEST evidence in this condition?

options.A: High-dose systemic corticosteroids (methylprednisolone 1-2mg/kg/day)
options.B: Immediate withdrawal of nevirapine + cyclosporine 3mg/kg/day
options.C: Immediate withdrawal of nevirapine + transfer to burns unit + IVIG 1g/kg/day x 3 days
options.D: Thalidomide 100mg/day + wound dressings

questions.explanation: Correct (C): This is Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN) - defined as >30% BSA epidermal detachment. Nevirapine is a classic causative drug. Management: (1) IMMEDIATE withdrawal of offending drug (critical - reduces mortality), (2) Transfer to burns/ICU unit for supportive care (IV fluids, wound care, thermoregulation, nutritional support), (3) IVIG in high doses (1g/kg/day x 3 days) is the most evidence-supported immunotherapy - inhibits Fas-FasL mediated keratinocyte apoptosis. SCORTEN 4 = approximately 58% mortality. Incorrect (A): Systemic corticosteroids are CONTRAINDICATED in TEN - increase risk of sepsis and delay healing. Incorrect (B): Cyclosporine has emerging evidence (especially in SJS) but is not the current first-line immunotherapy over IVIG in TEN. Also, drug withdrawal + cyclosporine alone is incomplete management. Incorrect (D): Thalidomide was tried in TEN and caused INCREASED MORTALITY in trials - absolutely contraindicated. EXAM PEARL: SJS = <10% BSA; SJS/TEN overlap = 10-30%; TEN = >30%. SCORTEN prognostic score: age>40, malignancy, HR>120, initial BSA>10%, urea>10, glucose>14, bicarb<20 - each = 1 point. Common drugs: sulfonamides, allopurinol, lamotrigine, nevirapine, NSAIDs, carbamazepine.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.image_title: Dermoscopy of a pigmented lesion showing atypical pigment network and irregular streaks
key_findings: Regression structures (white scar-like areas and blue-grey peppering)
questions.question_text: A 54-year-old fair-skinned man presents with a changing pigmented lesion on the back. Dermoscopy is shown. Excision biopsy reveals superficial spreading melanoma with Breslow thickness of 1.8mm, no ulceration, mitotic rate 1/mm². Sentinel lymph node biopsy is negative. According to AJCC staging, how should he be managed?

options.A: Wide local excision with 2cm margin; observation only
options.B: Wide local excision with 2cm margin + adjuvant nivolumab or dabrafenib/trametinib (if BRAF mutant)
options.C: Wide local excision with 1cm margin + adjuvant PUVA therapy
options.D: Radical lymph node dissection + interferon alpha-2b for 1 year

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Breslow thickness 1.8mm, no ulceration, no mitoses >1, negative SLNB = Stage IIA melanoma (T2bN0M0 or T3aN0M0). Management: Wide local excision with 2cm margin + consideration of adjuvant therapy. Current NCCN guidelines recommend adjuvant immunotherapy (nivolumab or pembrolizumab) or targeted therapy (dabrafenib + trametinib if BRAF V600 mutant) for Stage IIB-IIC and Stage III melanoma. For Stage IIA, adjuvant pembrolizumab is now an option based on KEYNOTE-716 data. Incorrect (A): Observation alone is insufficient given intermediate-high risk thickness - adjuvant therapy is now standard for this stage. Incorrect (C): PUVA has no role in melanoma management. 1cm margin is insufficient for 1.8mm Breslow (requires 2cm). Incorrect (D): Completion lymph node dissection is no longer standard (MSLT-II trial showed no OS benefit). Interferon is largely replaced by immunotherapy. EXAM PEARL: Breslow thickness determines margins: <1mm = 1cm, 1-2mm = 1-2cm, >2mm = 2cm. BRAF V600E mutation in ~50% melanomas. ABCDE rule: Asymmetry, Border, Colour, Diameter>6mm, Evolution.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A 30-year-old woman presents with an itchy papular rash appearing on sun-exposed areas within 30 minutes of sun exposure. The rash resolves completely within hours of avoiding sunlight. She has no family history of photosensitivity. Phototesting with UVA and UVB shows positive response to UVA. Which is the MOST likely diagnosis?

options.A: Polymorphic light eruption (PLE)
options.B: Solar urticaria
options.C: Chronic actinic dermatitis
options.D: Lupus erythematosus

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Solar urticaria presents with urticarial wheals/papular rash appearing within minutes (typically 5-30 minutes) of sun exposure and resolving completely within 1-2 hours of sun avoidance. IgE-mediated mechanism. UVA is the most common action spectrum. Incorrect (A): Polymorphic light eruption (PLE) - most common photodermatosis - presents with rash appearing hours after exposure, lasts days, and does NOT resolve within hours. It typically occurs in spring/early summer (hardening phenomenon). Incorrect (C): Chronic actinic dermatitis - persistent eczematous eruption in elderly men, persists even in covered areas, abnormal response to UVB, UVA, and visible light. Not transient. Incorrect (D): Lupus photosensitivity causes malar rash or discoid lesions - not transient urticarial papules. EXAM PEARL: Solar urticaria = wheals within minutes + resolve within 2 hours = IgE mediated = treat with antihistamines + sunscreens. PLE = papules/vesicles hours after exposure + lasts days = CMI mediated = treat with NB-UVB hardening therapy in spring.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A 72-year-old woman presents with intensely pruritic, tense blisters on normal and erythematous skin of the trunk and limbs. Nikolsky sign is negative. ELISA shows anti-BP180 antibodies at high titre. Histology shows subepidermal blistering with eosinophilic infiltrate. Which of the following statements about immunofluorescence findings is CORRECT?

options.A: Direct IF: IgG in fishnet pattern in epidermis; Indirect IF: positive on monkey esophagus
options.B: Direct IF: Linear IgG and C3 at DEJ; Salt-split skin shows IgG on epidermal side (roof)
options.C: Direct IF: IgA at dermal papillae tips; Indirect IF: positive on salt-split skin (dermal side)
options.D: Direct IF: Granular IgG at DEJ; Indirect IF: positive on monkey esophagus

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Bullous Pemphigoid (BP) - Direct IF shows linear IgG and C3 at the dermoepidermal junction (lamina lucida). On 1M NaCl salt-split skin: antibodies bind to the ROOF (epidermal side) because BP antigens (BP180/BPAG2, BP230/BPAG1) are located in the hemidesmosome/lamina lucida. This is the key differentiating test from EBA. Incorrect (A): Fishnet IgG in epidermis = Pemphigus Vulgaris; Indirect IF positive on monkey esophagus = Pemphigus. Incorrect (C): IgA at dermal papillae = Dermatitis Herpetiformis; dermal side on salt-split = Epidermolysis Bullosa Acquisita (EBA) which has IgG to collagen VII. Incorrect (D): Granular IgG at DEJ = Bullous SLE or EBA. EXAM PEARL: Salt-split skin test: ROOF = BP, Pemphigoid gestationis; FLOOR (dermal side) = EBA, Bullous SLE. BP180 = key antigen; BP antibody titre correlates with disease activity. BP is most common autoimmune bullous disorder in elderly.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A 45-year-old man from Rajasthan presents with a painless, slowly enlarging ulcer on the cheek with indurated, rolled edges and a granulating base, present for 4 months. He gives history of a preceding papule that broke down. Slit skin smear from the edge shows Leishman-Donovan bodies. He is diagnosed with cutaneous leishmaniasis. What is the treatment of choice for this presentation?

options.A: Oral miltefosine 100mg/day for 28 days
options.B: Intralesional sodium stibogluconate (SSG) weekly injections
options.C: Systemic sodium stibogluconate 20mg/kg/day IM for 20 days
options.D: Topical paromomycin ointment for 20 days

questions.explanation: Correct (B): For localized cutaneous leishmaniasis (single or few lesions, not disfiguring location, not immunocompromised), intralesional sodium stibogluconate (pentavalent antimonials) is the treatment of choice. It delivers high drug concentration locally with minimal systemic toxicity. Weekly injections until healing (typically 4-6 sessions). Incorrect (A): Oral miltefosine is used for visceral leishmaniasis primarily, and for cutaneous disease resistant to intralesional therapy or with multiple/large lesions - not first-line for a single localized lesion. Incorrect (C): Systemic SSG is reserved for multiple lesions, mucocutaneous disease, visceral involvement, or intralesional therapy failure. Higher systemic toxicity (cardiotoxicity, pancreatitis, hepatotoxicity). Incorrect (D): Topical paromomycin may be used for small/superficial lesions in non-disfiguring areas but has variable efficacy and is not standard for a 4-month indurated facial ulcer. EXAM PEARL: CL species: L. tropica (Old World, dry form, Oriental sore, self-healing), L. major (wet/rural form), L. donovani (Indian VL), L. braziliensis (New World, mucocutaneous). Leishmania diagnostic: smear from edge (not base), culture in NNN medium, PCR.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A 55-year-old woman presents with a 3-month history of proximal muscle weakness, difficulty rising from a chair, and dysphagia. Examination reveals heliotrope rash around both eyes, Gottron's papules over MCP and PIP joints, and V-sign erythema on chest. CK is 3500 U/L. MRI thighs shows muscle edema. A CT chest/abdomen/pelvis is performed and shows a 2cm spiculated lung mass. Which antibody is MOST likely to be positive and what does it indicate?

options.A: Anti-Jo-1; associated with antisynthetase syndrome and ILD
options.B: Anti-TIF1-γ (anti-p155/140); strongly associated with underlying malignancy
options.C: Anti-Mi-2; associated with classic dermatomyositis with good prognosis
options.D: Anti-MDA5; associated with amyopathic DM and rapidly progressive ILD

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Anti-TIF1-γ (transcription intermediary factor 1-gamma; anti-p155/140) has the strongest association with cancer-associated myositis. In adults with DM and this antibody, risk of underlying malignancy is significantly elevated (especially ovarian, lung, GI cancers). The CT finding of a lung mass confirms paraneoplastic DM. Incorrect (A): Anti-Jo-1 is the most common myositis-specific antibody - associated with antisynthetase syndrome (myositis + ILD + mechanic's hands + Raynaud's + arthritis), NOT particularly with malignancy. Incorrect (C): Anti-Mi-2 is associated with classic 'textbook' DM (V-sign, shawl sign, Gottron's papules), generally good treatment response and low malignancy risk. Incorrect (D): Anti-MDA5 is associated with amyopathic (clinically amyopathic) DM, very high risk of rapidly progressive ILD (can be fatal), skin ulceration, and palmar papules. EXAM PEARL: Malignancy in DM is most common at 55-65 years, especially in skin DM > anti-TIF1γ positive. Screen all adult onset DM for malignancy. MSAs (myositis-specific antibodies) determine phenotype, prognosis, and treatment response.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A 68-year-old diabetic man presents with severe burning pain in a dermatomal distribution on the right side of his chest for 3 days, followed by appearance of grouped vesicles on an erythematous base along T5-T6 dermatome. He reports significant allodynia. Which of the following statements about prevention of postherpetic neuralgia (PHN) is MOST accurate?

options.A: Early antiviral therapy (within 72 hours) with valacyclovir reduces the incidence and severity of PHN
options.B: Intralesional steroids at the time of rash onset prevent PHN
options.C: Topical acyclovir cream is equally effective as oral valacyclovir in preventing PHN
options.D: Gabapentin started early prevents PHN completely

questions.explanation: Correct (A): Early antiviral therapy (acyclovir/valacyclovir/famciclovir within 72 hours of rash onset, or any time if new vesicles still forming) reduces viral replication, shortens duration, reduces severity of acute pain, and most importantly reduces the incidence and severity of PHN. Valacyclovir (1g TID x7d) and famciclovir are preferred for better bioavailability. Incorrect (B): Intralesional steroids have no proven role in PHN prevention. Systemic steroids may reduce acute pain but do not prevent PHN. Incorrect (C): Topical acyclovir cream has negligible systemic absorption and is ineffective for dermatomal herpes zoster; oral/IV antivirals are required. Incorrect (D): Gabapentin and pregabalin treat established PHN - they do not prevent it. EXAM PEARL: PHN risk factors: age >60, severe acute pain, severe rash, ophthalmic HZ. Prevention: antiviral within 72h + Shingrix vaccine (recombinant subunit, preferred over Zostavax live attenuated). PHN treatment: topical lidocaine, capsaicin, tricyclic antidepressants, gabapentin/pregabalin, opioids.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A 55-year-old man with chronic renal failure on hemodialysis is noted to have a characteristic nail finding: the proximal half of the nail is white (leukonychia) and the distal half is pink/red-brown with a sharp demarcation line. What is this finding called and what is its underlying mechanism?

options.A: Terry's nails; due to hepatic cirrhosis causing hypoalbuminemia and edema
options.B: Lindsay's nails (half and half nails); due to increased melanin in distal nail bed with chronic renal failure
options.C: Muehrcke's nails; due to hypoalbuminemia causing paired transverse white bands
options.D: Beau's lines; due to temporary arrest of nail matrix growth during systemic illness

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Lindsay's nails (half-and-half nails) - proximal white half + distal pink/brown half with sharp demarcation. Classically associated with chronic renal failure. Mechanism: increased melanin deposition in distal nail bed (likely due to elevated MSH/ACTH in renal failure). Incorrect (A): Terry's nails - nail appears white/ground glass with only narrow 1-2mm distal pink band - associated with cirrhosis, CHF, diabetes, hypoalbuminemia. The description here with sharp midpoint demarcation is not Terry's. Incorrect (C): Muehrcke's nails - paired transverse white bands that disappear with blanching pressure (vascular origin) - associated with hypoalbuminemia but appear as bands, not half-and-half. Incorrect (D): Beau's lines = transverse grooves (not colour change) from temporary matrix arrest - seen after severe illness, chemotherapy, COVID-19. EXAM PEARL: Nail signs memory: Terry's = 2/3 white = cirrhosis/CHF; Lindsay's = half and half = CRF; Muehrcke's = paired white bands = hypoalbuminemia; Mees' lines = single transverse white bands = arsenic/heavy metal poisoning; Yellow nail syndrome = yellow + lymphedema + pleural effusion.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A 32-year-old woman presents with symmetrical brown patches on both cheeks, forehead, and upper lip. She is 28 weeks pregnant. Wood's lamp examination shows enhancement of pigmentation. She requests treatment. Which is the SAFEST and MOST appropriate management during pregnancy?

options.A: Start hydroquinone 4% cream + tretinoin 0.05% cream
options.B: Strict photoprotection with SPF 50+ broad-spectrum sunscreen and physical blockers
options.C: Oral tranexamic acid 250mg twice daily
options.D: Chemical peel with 20% trichloroacetic acid

questions.explanation: Correct (B): In pregnancy, melasma is exacerbated by hormonal changes and UV exposure. The SAFEST intervention is strict sun protection: broad-spectrum SPF 50+ sunscreen with physical blockers (zinc oxide/titanium dioxide). Many patients show significant improvement post-partum. Most topical agents have limited safety data in pregnancy. Incorrect (A): Hydroquinone is FDA Category C (animal studies show harm) - use should be avoided in pregnancy. Tretinoin is Category C/X - contraindicated in pregnancy (systemic retinoids are teratogenic; topical tretinoin has low absorption but is generally avoided). Incorrect (C): Oral tranexamic acid - safety not established in pregnancy; anti-fibrinolytic with potential thrombotic risk. Not recommended during pregnancy. Incorrect (D): Chemical peels can cause unpredictable inflammation and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation; not recommended in pregnancy, especially second/third trimester. EXAM PEARL: Melasma treatment hierarchy: Sunscreen → Hydroquinone (first-line after pregnancy) → Triple combination (HQ + tretinoin + mild steroid = Kligman's formula) → Tranexamic acid (oral/topical) → Chemical peels → Q-switched Nd:YAG laser.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A newborn girl is encased in a tight, shiny, parchment-like membrane with severe ectropion, eclabium, and flexion deformities at birth. The membrane cracks and peels over the next 2-3 weeks. She is subsequently found to have ichthyosis. Her affected brother has the same condition; her parents are unaffected. Which type of ichthyosis is MOST likely and what enzyme is deficient?

options.A: Ichthyosis vulgaris; filaggrin mutation (semi-dominant inheritance)
options.B: X-linked ichthyosis; steroid sulfatase deficiency
options.C: Lamellar ichthyosis; transglutaminase-1 (TGM1) deficiency (autosomal recessive)
options.D: Epidermolytic ichthyosis; keratin 1/10 mutation (autosomal dominant)

questions.explanation: Correct (C): 'Collodion baby' (shiny parchment membrane at birth + ectropion + eclabium) most commonly evolves into Lamellar Ichthyosis (LI). The autosomal recessive inheritance pattern (affected siblings, unaffected parents) fits. Most common mutation = TGM1 (transglutaminase-1) deficiency, essential for cornified envelope formation. Incorrect (A): Ichthyosis vulgaris is the most common ichthyosis, autosomal semi-dominant, associated with filaggrin mutations and atopy. It does NOT present as collodion baby; onset in first year of life with fine white scales. Incorrect (B): X-linked ichthyosis - steroid sulfatase deficiency, affects males only (X-linked recessive). Presents with large brown adherent scales, sparing palms/soles. NOT a collodion baby. Incorrect (D): Epidermolytic ichthyosis (bullous congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma) - autosomal dominant, keratin 1/10 mutations, presents with blistering in neonates then develops verrucous scales. Different from collodion phenotype. EXAM PEARL: Collodion baby = collodion membrane at birth. 80% evolve to LI or CIE. 10% become 'self-healing collodion baby'. Harlequin ichthyosis = most severe (ABCA12 mutation), armor plate-like scales, high mortality.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.image_title: Dermoscopy of a pearly nodule on the nose showing arborizing vessels
questions.question_text: A 65-year-old man with extensive sun damage presents with a pearly, translucent nodule with telangiectasias and central ulceration on the alar of the nose. Dermoscopy is shown. Shave biopsy confirms nodular basal cell carcinoma. Which of the following treatment modalities is MOST appropriate for this high-risk location BCC?

options.A: Cryotherapy
options.B: Mohs micrographic surgery
options.C: Imiquimod 5% cream for 6 weeks
options.D: Curettage and electrodesiccation

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Mohs micrographic surgery (MMS) is the treatment of choice for BCCs in high-risk locations (H-zone: periorbital, perinasal, periauricular, perioral, hands, feet, genitalia), large tumors (>2cm), recurrent tumors, poorly defined margins, aggressive histological subtypes, and immunosuppressed patients. The nose alar is in the H-zone with high recurrence risk if margins are inadequate. MMS provides highest cure rate (99%) with maximum tissue conservation. Incorrect (A): Cryotherapy is appropriate for small, superficial, well-defined BCCs on low-risk sites in elderly/poor surgical candidates. Not appropriate for high-risk location, nodular ulcerated BCC. Incorrect (C): Imiquimod (topical immune response modifier) is FDA-approved for superficial BCC only, not nodular BCC, and not in high-risk H-zone. Incorrect (D): Curettage and electrodesiccation is reserved for small (<1cm), superficial or nodular BCCs on low-risk areas (trunk, extremities); high recurrence rates on nose. EXAM PEARL: BCC = most common skin cancer. Associated with PTCH1 mutation (Hedgehog pathway). Risk areas: H-zone of face. Vismodegib/sonidegib (Hedgehog inhibitors) = for advanced/metastatic BCC. Never metastasizes except basosquamous variant.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A 24-year-old sexually active man presents with 5 days of urethral discharge and dysuria. Gram stain of urethral discharge shows Gram-negative intracellular diplococci within PMNs. NAAT confirms Neisseria gonorrhoeae. He also tests positive for Chlamydia trachomatis co-infection. What is the CURRENT recommended dual therapy?

options.A: Ciprofloxacin 500mg orally single dose + azithromycin 1g orally single dose
options.B: Ceftriaxone 500mg IM single dose + doxycycline 100mg BD for 7 days
options.C: Cefixime 400mg orally single dose + azithromycin 1g orally single dose
options.D: Spectinomycin 2g IM + erythromycin 500mg QID for 7 days

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Current CDC (2021) and WHO guidelines recommend Ceftriaxone 500mg IM single dose (increased from 250mg due to resistance) for gonorrhea, PLUS Doxycycline 100mg BD x7 days for chlamydia co-infection (azithromycin resistance in chlamydia has increased; doxycycline now preferred for non-pregnant patients). Incorrect (A): Ciprofloxacin resistance is now widespread in N. gonorrhoeae globally (especially in Southeast Asia/India) - fluoroquinolones are no longer recommended empirically for gonorrhea. Incorrect (C): Cefixime oral has lower and less reliable tissue levels than ceftriaxone IM; no longer first-line. When used (if IM not possible), higher dose (800mg) is recommended. Incorrect (D): Spectinomycin is unavailable in many countries and lacks efficacy against pharyngeal gonorrhea. Erythromycin is inferior to doxycycline for chlamydia. EXAM PEARL: NGU (non-gonococcal urethritis): C. trachomatis most common, also M. genitalium, Ureaplasma. Gonorrhea complications: epididymo-orchitis, PID, DGI (disseminated gonococcal infection = septic arthritis + skin lesions + tenosynovitis). Gram smear: 95% sensitive in symptomatic males, <50% in females.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A hairdresser presents with chronic relapsing dermatitis of the hands and forearms. She notes the rash worsens during work weeks and improves during holidays. Patch testing shows a positive reaction to paraphenylenediamine (PPD) at D48 and D96 with no reaction to nickel, rubber, or preservatives. What is the CORRECT interpretation and next step?

options.A: This is irritant contact dermatitis from repeated wet work; PPD reaction is false positive
options.B: She has allergic contact dermatitis to PPD (hair dye); she must avoid all PPD-containing products and cross-reactors (benzocaine, sulfonamides)
options.C: The positive patch test indicates Type I hypersensitivity; serum specific IgE should be measured
options.D: She should continue working with gloves only as the risk of systemic sensitization is low

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Positive patch test to PPD at 48 and 96 hours = Type IV (delayed) hypersensitivity = allergic contact dermatitis. PPD is the most common allergen in hair dyes. Management = complete avoidance of PPD and known cross-reactors: benzocaine (local anaesthetic), procaine, sulfonamides, sulfonyl urea drugs, PABA (sunscreen), azo dyes, thiuram. The hairdresser should be counseled about occupational hazard and possibly career change. Incorrect (A): Occupational hand dermatitis from wet work is predominantly irritant CD, but a positive patch test at both 48h and 96h indicates true sensitization (ACD). False positives to PPD are uncommon and the occupational history strongly supports ACD. Incorrect (C): Patch testing assesses Type IV (cell-mediated) delayed hypersensitivity - NOT Type I IgE-mediated. Serum specific IgE is for Type I allergy. Incorrect (D): Gloves are insufficient - PPD can penetrate standard gloves. Continued exposure will worsen sensitization and risk systemic contact dermatitis. EXAM PEARL: PPD allergy = cross-reacts with BAMBA (Benzocaine, Azo dyes, Meta-aminophenol, Benzidine-based dyes, Aniline compounds). Patch test = gold standard for ACD diagnosis. Read at 48h AND 96h to distinguish irritant (+) from true allergic (++).

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A 35-year-old man presents with intense nocturnal pruritus for 3 weeks. His wife and two children also have similar symptoms. Examination shows papules, vesicles, and linear burrows in web spaces of fingers, wrists, and periumbilical area. Which of the following is FIRST-LINE treatment and how should household contacts be managed?

options.A: Permethrin 5% cream applied from neck down, left for 8-12 hours, repeated after 1 week; all household contacts treated simultaneously
options.B: Lindane 1% lotion applied for 6 hours; treat only symptomatic contacts
options.C: Oral ivermectin 200mcg/kg single dose; no treatment needed for asymptomatic contacts
options.D: Benzyl benzoate 25% applied for 24 hours; repeat daily for 3 days

questions.explanation: Correct (A): Permethrin 5% cream is the first-line treatment for scabies. Applied from neck downward (head included in infants, elderly, immunocompromised) for 8-12 hours, then washed off. Repeated after 1 week (second application kills mites that hatched from eggs after first treatment). ALL household contacts and sexual contacts must be treated simultaneously (even if asymptomatic) to prevent reinfection - this is critical. Incorrect (B): Lindane is now avoided/restricted due to neurotoxicity (seizure risk in children, pregnant women). Treating only symptomatic contacts leads to reinfection cycles. Incorrect (C): Oral ivermectin is an alternative (not first-line in India for routine scabies) and is particularly useful for crusted/Norwegian scabies, institutional outbreaks, or when topical therapy fails. Asymptomatic contacts CAN be pre-emptively infected - all contacts should be treated. Incorrect (D): Benzyl benzoate 25% is a second-line agent (20% for children) - not first-line. Application for 24 hours causes more irritation. EXAM PEARL: Crusted (Norwegian) scabies = immunocompromised/elderly = thousands of mites = highly contagious = treat with combination oral ivermectin + topical permethrin. Post-scabetic itch can persist for 4-6 weeks after successful treatment (hypersensitivity reaction) - does not mean treatment failure.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A 40-year-old woman has had daily wheals for 8 months with angioedema. She has no identifiable triggers. ASST (autologous serum skin test) is positive. Her urticaria is not controlled with cetirizine 10mg daily. She has no contraindications to biologic therapy. According to current guidelines, what is the NEXT best step?

options.A: Add H2 antihistamine (ranitidine) to H1 antihistamine
options.B: Switch to first-generation antihistamine (chlorphenamine) for better sedation and histamine blockade
options.C: Updose cetirizine to 4x the licensed dose (40mg/day) as per EAACI guidelines
options.D: Start cyclosporine 3-5mg/kg/day as third-line therapy

questions.explanation: Correct (C): EAACI/GA2LEN/EDF/WAO guidelines for chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU) recommend a step-up approach: Step 1 = standard dose H1-AH → Step 2 = UPDOSE to 4x (omalizumab can be considered here or at step 3) → Step 3 = add omalizumab 300mg/month → Step 4 = cyclosporine. Updosing to 4x is the recommended NEXT step before adding omalizumab/biologics. The positive ASST suggests autoimmune urticaria (anti-FcεRI or anti-IgE antibodies). Incorrect (A): Adding H2 antihistamines (now ranitidine withdrawn; famotidine available) has limited evidence and is not currently in EAACI treatment algorithm as a standard step. Incorrect (B): First-generation (sedating) antihistamines are NOT preferred over second-generation due to side effect profile (sedation, anticholinergic effects) and are not recommended by current guidelines for CSU. Incorrect (D): Cyclosporine is a 4th-line option (after standard dose AH → 4x dose AH → omalizumab fail). Using it before updosing and before omalizumab is premature. EXAM PEARL: CSU = wheals >6 weeks, no identifiable cause. ASST positive = autoimmune urticaria. Omalizumab (anti-IgE) = 300mg SC monthly = treatment of choice for refractory CSU. Urticaria activity score (UAS7) monitors disease severity.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A 30-year-old man presents with a painful genital ulcer on the penile shaft for 5 days. He has had 3 new sexual partners in the past month. Examination shows a single, well-defined, deep ulcer with undermined/ragged edges and a necrotic grey base. The base is very tender. Inguinal lymph nodes are enlarged, tender, and begin to show fluctuance. Gram stain from the ulcer base shows 'school of fish' pattern of gram-negative bacilli. What is the diagnosis and treatment?

options.A: Syphilis (Treponema pallidum); benzathine penicillin 2.4 MU IM
options.B: Chancroid (Haemophilus ducreyi); azithromycin 1g single dose or ciprofloxacin 500mg BD x3 days
options.C: Herpes genitalis (HSV-2); acyclovir 400mg TID x7 days
options.D: Donovanosis (Klebsiella granulomatis); doxycycline 100mg BD for 3 weeks

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Chancroid (soft sore) is caused by Haemophilus ducreyi. Classic features: painful, deep ulcer with undermined/ragged/irregular edges + necrotic grey/yellow base + very painful inguinal lymphadenopathy (bubo) that can suppurate and rupture. Gram stain: gram-negative coccobacilli in 'school of fish/railway track' pattern. Treatment: Azithromycin 1g single dose (preferred) OR ciprofloxacin 500mg BD x3 days OR ceftriaxone 250mg IM single dose. Incorrect (A): Syphilitic chancre = PAINLESS, indurated, clean base, regular edges. Gram stain not useful for T. pallidum (spirochete, not seen on Gram). Lymph nodes are non-tender in primary syphilis. Incorrect (C): Herpetic ulcers = multiple, shallow, vesicular, very painful. No undermined edges. Gram stain shows no bacteria; Tzanck smear shows multinucleated giant cells. Incorrect (D): Donovanosis = progressive painless genital ulceration with 'beef-red' friable granulation tissue. Tissue crush prep/biopsy shows Donovan bodies. No lymphadenopathy typically. EXAM PEARL: Painful genital ulcers = Herpes + Chancroid + LGV (secondary stage). Painless = Syphilis + Donovanosis. Chancroid + HIV co-infection is common - always test. Bubo = fluctuant LN = aspirate (do NOT incise).

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A 38-year-old man with severe plaque psoriasis (PASI 28, BSA 35%) failed methotrexate and cyclosporine. His dermatologist plans to initiate a biologic. Pre-screening reveals: QuantiFERON-TB Gold POSITIVE, HIV negative, Hepatitis B surface antigen NEGATIVE, anti-HBs antibody NEGATIVE (not vaccinated), Hepatitis C antibody negative, recent CXR normal. What is the MOST appropriate management before starting the biologic?

options.A: Start secukinumab immediately; LTBI treatment is not required for IL-17 inhibitors
options.B: Treat LTBI with isoniazid 300mg daily for 9 months before starting any biologic
options.C: Treat LTBI (isoniazid 300mg/day x9 months or rifampicin x4 months) concurrent with biologic after 4 weeks; vaccinate against Hepatitis B
options.D: Start ustekinumab only (IL-12/23 inhibitor has low TB risk); no LTBI treatment needed

questions.explanation: Correct (C): LTBI (positive QuantiFERON, normal CXR, no active TB) requires prophylactic treatment before/concurrent with all biologics that significantly impair immunity (anti-TNF, anti-IL12/23, anti-IL-17, anti-IL-23). Current guidelines: Start LTBI treatment (INH x9m OR rifampicin x4m) at least 4 weeks before initiating biologic. Biologic can be started after 4 weeks of LTBI therapy (not necessary to complete full course first). Additionally, this patient is anti-HBs negative and HBsAg negative = susceptible to HBV - should receive Hepatitis B vaccination before/during biologic therapy. Incorrect (A): All biologics carry TB risk - IL-17 inhibitors (secukinumab, ixekizumab) have somewhat lower TB risk than anti-TNF but LTBI treatment is still recommended. Incorrect (B): Waiting 9 months before starting biologic unnecessarily delays treatment for severe psoriasis. Concurrent initiation after 4 weeks is acceptable per guidelines. Incorrect (D): Ustekinumab has lower TB reactivation risk than anti-TNF but LTBI treatment is still required. EXAM PEARL: TB screening mandatory before ALL biologics. Anti-TNF (adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab) = highest TB risk. Biologics for psoriasis: Anti-TNF → Anti-IL12/23 (ustekinumab) → Anti-IL17 (secukinumab, ixekizumab) → Anti-IL23 (guselkumab, risankizumab, tildrakizumab).

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A 7-year-old boy presents with patchy hair loss on the scalp with broken-off hairs at follicular orifices, giving a 'black dot' pattern. Scaling is present. Wood's lamp examination shows NO fluorescence. KOH of broken hairs shows spores within the hair shaft (endothrix pattern). What is the MOST likely causative organism and treatment of choice?

options.A: Microsporum canis; griseofulvin for 6-8 weeks (Wood's lamp: bright green fluorescence)
options.B: Trichophyton tonsurans; oral griseofulvin for 6-8 weeks (or terbinafine)
options.C: Trichophyton violaceum; topical clotrimazole for 4 weeks
options.D: Microsporum audouinii; itraconazole pulse therapy

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Black dot tinea capitis with endothrix pattern (spores inside hair shaft) + NO Wood's lamp fluorescence = Trichophyton tonsurans (most common in North America/Asia). Treatment = oral griseofulvin 20-25mg/kg/day for 6-8 weeks (drug of choice traditionally) OR oral terbinafine (especially effective for Trichophyton species). Topical antifungals are INADEQUATE as they cannot penetrate the hair shaft. Incorrect (A): Microsporum canis causes ectothrix infection (spores outside hair shaft) with bright green Wood's lamp fluorescence. Wrong organism and fluorescence pattern for this case. Incorrect (C): Topical antifungals are insufficient for tinea capitis - oral therapy is mandatory. Trichophyton violaceum does cause black dot TC but topical treatment alone is wrong. Incorrect (D): Microsporum audouinii causes grey patch TC (ectothrix) with green fluorescence. Itraconazole pulse is not standard first-line for tinea capitis. EXAM PEARL: Wood's lamp fluorescence: Microsporum species = green ('ECM-M' fluorescent); Trichophyton = NO fluorescence. Tinea capitis treatment always requires ORAL antifungal. Adjunctive selenium sulfide/ketoconazole shampoo reduces spread. Kerion = intense inflammatory response to dermatophyte = treat with antifungal ± steroids.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A 45-year-old woman has had Raynaud's phenomenon for 3 years. She now presents with tightening of facial and hand skin, dysphagia, and exertional breathlessness. PFTs show FVC 58%, DLCO 45% of predicted. Capillaroscopy shows giant capillaries and avascular areas. ANA is positive; anti-Scl70 (anti-topoisomerase I) is strongly positive. HRCT chest shows bilateral basal subpleural reticulation and honeycombing. What is the MOST appropriate treatment for her lung disease?

options.A: High-dose prednisolone 1mg/kg/day
options.B: Mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) 3g/day; nintedanib if progressive
options.C: Methotrexate and hydroxychloroquine combination
options.D: Cyclophosphamide IV pulse monthly for 6 months

questions.explanation: Correct (B): This is diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis (dcSSc) with ILD (FVC <70%, significant DLCO reduction, HRCT showing UIP/NSIP pattern). Anti-Scl70 = dcSSc, high risk of ILD progression. Current first-line treatment for SSc-ILD = Mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) - based on SLS-II trial showing non-inferiority to cyclophosphamide with better safety profile. Nintedanib (anti-fibrotic, tyrosine kinase inhibitor) is added/used for progressive SSc-ILD (SENSCIS trial). Incorrect (A): High-dose steroids in SSc can precipitate scleroderma renal crisis (especially >15mg prednisolone) - relatively contraindicated. Low-dose steroids may be used for inflammatory features but NOT for ILD. Incorrect (C): Methotrexate is used for skin disease in early dcSSc, not for ILD. Hydroxychloroquine does not have proven efficacy in SSc-ILD. Incorrect (D): IV cyclophosphamide was previously first-line (SLS-I trial) but is now second-line/alternative to MMF due to greater toxicity (hemorrhagic cystitis, gonadotoxicity, malignancy risk). EXAM PEARL: Anti-centromere = limited SSc (CREST) = PAH risk. Anti-Scl70 = diffuse SSc = ILD risk. Anti-RNA polymerase III = renal crisis risk. SSc renal crisis = hypertensive emergency = ACE inhibitors (drug of choice). PAH in SSc = endothelin receptor antagonists, PDE5 inhibitors.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A 60-year-old immunosuppressed kidney transplant recipient on tacrolimus presents with a rapidly growing, indurated, crusted plaque with central ulceration on the dorsum of the right hand. Biopsy shows moderately differentiated SCC with perineural invasion (PNI). What is the management and why is this patient at particularly high risk?

options.A: Cryotherapy; immunosuppression does not significantly alter SCC behaviour
options.B: Wide local excision with 4mm margin; PNI does not affect prognosis if margins are clear
options.C: Mohs micrographic surgery (or wide excision with 6-10mm margin) + adjuvant radiotherapy; consider reduction of immunosuppression; high metastatic risk due to transplant status and PNI
options.D: Imiquimod 5% cream for 12 weeks followed by curettage

questions.explanation: Correct (C): This is a HIGH-RISK SCC - high-risk factors include: organ transplant recipient (OTR) status, rapid growth, perineural invasion (PNI), location on hand (high-risk site), immunosuppression. In OTRs, SCC is 60-100x more common and behaves more aggressively with higher metastatic potential (~5-8% vs <2% in immunocompetent). Management: Mohs surgery or wide excision with adequate margins (6-10mm for high-risk SCC) + adjuvant radiotherapy for PNI/nodal spread. Consider switching immunosuppression from calcineurin inhibitors to mTOR inhibitors (sirolimus) which have antiproliferative effects. Incorrect (A): Cryotherapy is completely inadequate for invasive, high-risk SCC with PNI. Immunosuppression dramatically worsens SCC prognosis. Incorrect (B): PNI is a HIGH-RISK feature increasing recurrence and metastatic risk. Clear margins alone are insufficient - adjuvant RT should be considered. Incorrect (D): Imiquimod is for actinic keratosis and superficial SCC in situ - absolutely inadequate for invasive SCC with PNI. EXAM PEARL: High-risk SCC features: size >2cm, depth >4mm, location (lip/ear/genitalia), PNI, lymphovascular invasion, poor differentiation, OTR status, recurrence. Actinic keratosis = premalignant precursor. Field cancerization in OTRs = widespread actinic damage.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A 28-year-old farmer from Maharashtra presents with a painless swelling on the foot with multiple sinuses discharging yellowish granules. X-ray shows bone destruction and 'punched out' lesions. Histology of the granule shows broad aseptate hyphae with a 'sunset appearance' (chlamydoconidia at hyphal tips). Gram stain of granule is negative. What is the diagnosis and treatment of choice?

options.A: Actinomycetoma (Nocardia); co-trimoxazole + amikacin
options.B: Eumycetoma (Madurella mycetomatis); itraconazole 400mg/day for months to years ± surgery
options.C: Chromoblastomycosis (Fonsecaea pedrosoi); itraconazole for 12 months
options.D: Sporotrichosis (Sporothrix schenckii); oral itraconazole for 3-6 months

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Classic presentation of Eumycetoma (Madura foot): chronic painless swelling + sinuses + grain discharge. Yellow/white large (>2mm) grains = Madurella mycetomatis (most common in India). Histology shows broad fungal hyphae. Gram stain negative (fungal wall not gram-positive). Treatment: Itraconazole 400mg/day for prolonged periods (12-24 months or longer) ± surgical debulking. Voriconazole is an alternative. No cure with drugs alone often - combined medical + surgical approach. Incorrect (A): Actinomycetoma (bacterial: Nocardia, Actinomadura, Streptomyces) - Gram stain POSITIVE (gram-positive filamentous bacteria). Small grains (<1mm), white/yellow/red depending on organism. Treatment = antibiotics (co-trimoxazole, amikacin). No antifungals. Incorrect (C): Chromoblastomycosis = verrucous/warty skin lesions (no sinuses, no bone), 'medlar bodies' (sclerotic cells/copper pennies) on histology. Sinuses and bone destruction are NOT features. Incorrect (D): Sporotrichosis = lymphocutaneous disease along lymphatics after thorn prick, asteroid bodies on histology. No sinuses or bone destruction. EXAM PEARL: Mycetoma triad = painless swelling + sinuses + grain discharge. Grains: white = Pseudallescheria boydii (eumycetoma) or Actinomadura madurae; black = Madurella mycetomatis; yellow/red = various actinomycetes. Investigation of choice = grain examination (nature determines treatment).

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: An 8-year-old boy is brought by his parents for evaluation of multiple light brown macules over his trunk. On examination: 7 café-au-lait macules (largest = 3cm), axillary freckles (Crowe's sign), and a small nodule on the iris seen on slit lamp examination. His father has similar skin findings. Which diagnosis does he have and which surveillance is MOST important?

options.A: McCune-Albright syndrome; surveillance for polyostotic fibrous dysplasia and endocrinopathy
options.B: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1); annual ophthalmology exam, BP monitoring, neurological assessment
options.C: Neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2); annual MRI brain for acoustic neuromas
options.D: Legius syndrome; surveillance for CNS tumors

questions.explanation: Correct (B): NF1 diagnosis requires ≥2 of 7 NIH criteria. This boy has: ≥6 CALMs >5mm (prepubertal), axillary freckling (Crowe's sign), and Lisch nodules (iris hamartomas on slit lamp). Plus family history (father affected) = autosomal dominant. Surveillance: annual ophthalmology (optic glioma - most common CNS tumor in NF1), BP monitoring (renovascular hypertension, pheochromocytoma), neurodevelopmental assessment, scoliosis screening. Incorrect (A): McCune-Albright = IRREGULAR ('coast of Maine') CALMs + polyostotic fibrous dysplasia + endocrinopathy (precocious puberty). No iris nodules, no freckling, no family history (somatic mutation). Incorrect (C): NF2 - bilateral acoustic neuromas, meningiomas, spinal ependymomas. Skin lesions minimal - few CALMs, plaque-like neurofibromas. NO Lisch nodules. Chromosome 22, not 17. Incorrect (D): Legius syndrome (SPRED1 mutation) mimics NF1 with CALMs and freckling but NO Lisch nodules, neurofibromas, or CNS tumors - benign condition. EXAM PEARL: NF1 gene = chromosome 17q11.2 (neurofibromin - tumor suppressor). NF2 = chromosome 22 (merlin/schwannomin). Plexiform neurofibroma in NF1 = pathognomonic, can undergo malignant transformation to MPNST.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A 35-year-old woman presents with palpable purpura on lower legs, arthralgia, and haematuria. She had an upper respiratory tract infection 2 weeks ago. Urinalysis shows RBC casts. Skin biopsy shows leukocytoclastic vasculitis with IgA deposits on direct immunofluorescence. What is the diagnosis and its classification in the ACR nomenclature?

options.A: Polyarteritis nodosa; medium vessel vasculitis
options.B: IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein Purpura); small vessel vasculitis (immune complex mediated)
options.C: ANCA-associated vasculitis (GPA); small vessel vasculitis
options.D: Cryoglobulinemic vasculitis; associated with Hepatitis C

questions.explanation: Correct (B): IgA vasculitis (HSP) - classic triad: palpable purpura (lower limbs) + arthralgia/arthritis + renal involvement (IgA nephropathy). Post-streptococcal/viral trigger. DIF shows IgA deposits in vessel walls = pathognomonic. ACR classification: small vessel vasculitis, immune complex mediated. Most common systemic vasculitis in children. Incorrect (A): Polyarteritis nodosa = medium vessel vasculitis = no IgA deposits, no glomerulonephritis, associated with HBV, mononeuritis multiplex, microaneurysms. Incorrect (C): GPA (Wegener's) = ANCA-associated (PR3-ANCA) = pauci-immune (NO immune deposits on DIF) = upper airway + lung + kidney involvement. NOT IgA deposits. Incorrect (D): Cryoglobulinemic vasculitis = associated with HCV, mixed cryoglobulins = purpura + neuropathy + arthralgia. DIF shows IgG/IgM deposits, not IgA. EXAM PEARL: IgA vasculitis: GI symptoms (intussusception in children), scrotal involvement in boys. Renal involvement = poor prognostic factor. Treatment = supportive (NSAIDs for arthralgia), steroids for severe GI/renal disease. Adults have worse renal prognosis than children.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A 30-year-old man with plaque psoriasis has troublesome psoriasis of the scalp unresponsive to tar shampoo and mild topical steroids. He also has psoriasis of the flexures (groin, axillae) causing significant discomfort. What is the MOST appropriate topical management for his flexural psoriasis?

options.A: Very high potency topical steroid (clobetasol propionate 0.05%) twice daily long-term
options.B: Calcipotriol/betamethasone dipropionate gel twice daily
options.C: Tacrolimus 0.1% ointment or low-potency corticosteroid with rotation
options.D: Coal tar paste under occlusion nightly

questions.explanation: Correct (C): Flexural (inverse) psoriasis requires special treatment considerations. The skin of flexures is occluded, thin, and more permeable - high-potency steroids cause rapid skin atrophy, striae, and systemic absorption. Tacrolimus 0.1% ointment (or pimecrolimus 1% cream) = calcineurin inhibitors = anti-inflammatory without skin atrophy = ideal for flexures and face. Alternatively, low/mid-potency steroids used intermittently (not long-term) with rotation. Incorrect (A): Very high potency steroids in flexures cause rapid severe atrophy, striae, and may cause skin barrier breakdown leading to secondary infection. Absolutely inappropriate for long-term use in flexures. Incorrect (B): Calcipotriol/betamethasone dipropionate gel is approved for scalp (not specifically flexural) psoriasis; betamethasone component still carries atrophy risk in flexures. Incorrect (D): Coal tar is irritating to flexural skin and impractical/cosmetically unacceptable for groin/axillae. EXAM PEARL: Treat special sites carefully: Face/flexures/genitals = topical calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus, pimecrolimus) preferred. Scalp psoriasis = tar/selenium shampoo + salicylic acid gel + betamethasone valerate scalp lotion. Nail psoriasis = intralesional steroid into nail fold, tazarotene gel, biologics.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A 55-year-old diabetic man presents with thickened, discoloured, brittle toenails affecting the great toenails bilaterally. KOH examination of nail clippings shows fungal hyphae. Culture confirms Trichophyton rubrum. He is on atorvastatin. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate treatment?

options.A: Topical ciclopirox lacquer for 48 weeks
options.B: Oral terbinafine 250mg daily for 12 weeks (toenails)
options.C: Oral fluconazole 50mg daily for 6 months
options.D: Oral itraconazole pulse (400mg/day for 1 week/month) for 3 pulses

questions.explanation: Correct (B): For Trichophyton onychomycosis (dermatophyte), oral terbinafine is the drug of choice. Terbinafine 250mg/day for 6 weeks (fingernails) or 12 weeks (toenails) - fungicidal against dermatophytes, accumulates in nail. Cure rates ~70-80%. Minimal drug interactions with statins (CYP2D6 inhibitor, not CYP3A4, so minimal interaction with atorvastatin which uses CYP3A4). Incorrect (A): Topical ciclopirox lacquer has poor nail penetration and very low cure rates for established onychomycosis (<10%); suitable only for superficial white onychomycosis or as adjunct. Incorrect (C): Fluconazole 150mg weekly for 6-9 months (toenails) is an alternative but daily 50mg is suboptimal dosing and less effective than terbinafine for dermatophytes. Incorrect (D): Itraconazole pulse therapy is an alternative for non-dermatophyte molds or Candida onychomycosis; for dermatophytes, terbinafine is superior. Importantly, itraconazole is a potent CYP3A4 inhibitor - significant interaction risk with statins (myopathy). EXAM PEARL: DLSO (distal lateral subungual onychomycosis) = most common type = T. rubrum. SWO (superficial white onychomycosis) = T. mentagrophytes = topical treatment may suffice. Proximal subungual = HIV marker. Treatment monitoring: LFTs before and during terbinafine in patients with liver disease.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.image_title: Histopathology showing atypical lymphocytes in epidermis with Pautrier microabscesses
key_findings: Pautrier microabscesses (clusters of atypical lymphocytes in epidermis)
Band-like lymphocytic infiltrate in upper dermis
questions.question_text: A 62-year-old man presents with a 5-year history of chronic scaly pruritic patches on the trunk and buttocks, which his dermatologist diagnosed as 'chronic eczema' repeatedly. Skin biopsy is shown. Immunohistochemistry shows CD3+, CD4+, CD8-, CD20-, CD30- T-cells in the epidermis. Flow cytometry of peripheral blood shows no circulating Sézary cells. What is the stage and most appropriate treatment?

options.A: Sézary syndrome (Stage IVA); CHOP chemotherapy
options.B: Mycosis fungoides Stage IA-IB (patch/plaque stage); skin-directed therapy (NB-UVB, PUVA, topical steroids, topical mechlorethamine)
options.C: CD30+ lymphoproliferative disorder; brentuximab vedotin
options.D: Lymphomatoid papulosis; observation only as it is self-healing

questions.explanation: Correct (B): This is Mycosis Fungoides (MF) - most common cutaneous T-cell lymphoma. Classic features: patch/plaque stage (chronic eczema-like) → indolent course → histology shows Pautrier microabscesses + epidermotropic CD4+ T cells with cerebriform nuclei. No circulating Sézary cells = not Sézary syndrome. Patch/plaque stage (Stage IA: <10% BSA; Stage IB: ≥10% BSA) = skin-directed therapy: NB-UVB (patches), PUVA (plaques), topical corticosteroids, topical mechlorethamine (chlormethine gel - FDA approved). Excellent prognosis in early stage. Incorrect (A): Sézary syndrome = leukemic variant of MF = erythroderma + Sézary cells in blood (CD4:CD8 >10, >1000 Sézary cells/mm³). This patient has no circulating Sézary cells. CHOP is not standard first-line even for advanced MF. Incorrect (C): CD30 is NEGATIVE in this case. CD30+ CTCL (primary cutaneous anaplastic large cell lymphoma, lymphomatoid papulosis) are different entities requiring different management. Incorrect (D): Lymphomatoid papulosis = recurrent self-healing papulonodular lesions with CD30+ histology - different from this chronic patch/plaque disease. EXAM PEARL: MF stages: IA (<10% BSA patches/plaques) → IB (≥10%) → IIA + LN → IIB (tumor stage) → III (erythroderma) → IVA (LN/blood) → IVB (visceral). Prognosis excellent in IA; poor in IV. 'Footprint in snow' = epidermotropism on H&E.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A 35-year-old HIV-positive man (CD4 count 45 cells/µL, viral load 250,000 copies/mL) presents with violaceous nodular plaques on the trunk, face, and hard palate. He also has bilateral pedal edema. Biopsy shows spindle cells with vascular slit-like spaces and extravasated red blood cells. What is the treatment of choice for this systemic presentation?

options.A: Initiate ART immediately; local intralesional vinblastine for skin lesions
options.B: Systemic chemotherapy (liposomal doxorubicin) + concurrent ART initiation; monitor for IRIS
options.C: Imiquimod 5% cream to all skin lesions; delay ART until Kaposi's is controlled
options.D: Radiotherapy to all lesions; no role of ART in visceral KS

questions.explanation: Correct (B): This is AIDS-defining Kaposi's Sarcoma (KS) with systemic involvement (visceral/pulmonary KS suggested by pedal edema = lymphatic involvement/pulmonary KS), CD4 45 = advanced AIDS. HHV-8 (KSHV) is the causative agent. Systemic KS (T1 category per ACTG staging: tumor involving viscera/edema/extensive oral KS) = systemic chemotherapy + ART. Liposomal doxorubicin (or paclitaxel) is first-line systemic chemotherapy. ART (antiretroviral therapy) must be started concurrently - immune reconstitution is key to long-term remission. Monitor for IRIS (immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome) - KS can flare with ART initiation. Incorrect (A): Intralesional vinblastine is for isolated, limited cutaneous KS lesions only. ART alone may suffice for T0 (limited skin) KS, but not for systemic disease with edema. Incorrect (C): Imiquimod is for very limited skin KS patches in non-critical locations. Delaying ART in AIDS is dangerous and worsens immunosuppression and KS progression. Incorrect (D): Radiotherapy is used for localized KS (especially oral, facial, or symptomatic lesions) - not for systemic disease. ART is the cornerstone of KS management regardless of extent. EXAM PEARL: KS types: Classic (elderly Mediterranean men, indolent), African endemic, Iatrogenic (post-transplant), AIDS-associated (aggressive). HHV-8 seropositivity = risk factor. ACTG staging: T (tumor) + I (immune - CD4) + S (systemic symptoms).

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A 25-year-old woman presents with burning, redness, and papulopustular eruption on the face that worsens when she stops applying a cream she has been using for 2 years for 'skin whitening' purchased from a local market. Examination shows perioral sparing, multiple papules/pustules, and erythema. Telangiectasia is also noted. What is the diagnosis and management?

options.A: Acne rosacea; metronidazole gel and doxycycline
options.B: Topical corticosteroid-induced rosacea-like dermatitis (steroid rosacea); gradual withdrawal of steroid, oral tetracycline, and topical metronidazole
options.C: Perioral dermatitis; topical erythromycin and oral tetracycline
options.D: Seborrhoeic dermatitis; topical ketoconazole and low-potency steroid

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Classic presentation of topical corticosteroid abuse on face - skin whitening creams commonly contain potent/very potent topical steroids (often unlabeled). Features: burning/stinging on withdrawal ('addiction'), papulopustular eruption, erythema, telangiectasia = steroid rosacea. Management: GRADUAL withdrawal (abrupt withdrawal causes severe rebound) + oral tetracycline (doxycycline 100mg BD for 4-6 weeks) + topical metronidazole or azelaic acid. Incorrect (A): True rosacea has flushing, centrofacial distribution, trigger factors (spicy food, alcohol, temperature change) without prior steroid use history. This patient's history of prolonged cream use is the key distinguishing factor. However, management is similar - the diagnosis here specifically is steroid-induced rosacea. Incorrect (C): Perioral dermatitis presents with perioral papulopustules with perioral sparing (sparing of vermilion border) - similar appearance but specifically perioral/perinasal/periocular. This patient has widespread facial involvement. Also caused by topical steroid use. Incorrect (D): Seborrhoeic dermatitis shows greasy scales on nasolabial folds, eyebrows, scalp - different morphology. EXAM PEARL: Topical steroid side effects: Skin - atrophy, striae, telangiectasia, steroid rosacea, perioral dermatitis, acneiform eruption, purpura, impaired wound healing, enhanced infections. Systemic - HPA axis suppression, Cushingoid features, glaucoma, cataracts.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A 60-year-old diabetic woman presents with rapidly progressive swelling, pain, and bluish-purple discoloration of the left lower leg. There is crepitus on palpation and a foul-smelling discharge from a wound. She is febrile (39.5°C) and hypotensive. X-ray shows subcutaneous gas. What is the MOST appropriate management?

options.A: High-dose IV antibiotics (meropenem + clindamycin + vancomycin) and close monitoring
options.B: Emergency surgical debridement + broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (meropenem + clindamycin + vancomycin); consider hyperbaric oxygen
options.C: Urgent dermatology referral for wound biopsy and culture, then targeted antibiotics
options.D: IV antibiotics alone; surgery only if no improvement in 48 hours

questions.explanation: Correct (B): This is Necrotizing Fasciitis (NF) - a life-threatening surgical emergency. LRINEC score criteria: subcutaneous gas on X-ray + rapidly spreading + crepitus + systemic sepsis + diabetes = high index of suspicion. Management = IMMEDIATE (within hours) surgical debridement of ALL necrotic tissue (wide and deep), PLUS broad-spectrum IV antibiotics covering gram-positive (MRSA - vancomycin), gram-negative (meropenem), and anaerobes (clindamycin - also inhibits toxin production). Hyperbaric oxygen is adjunctive. Mortality 20-40% even with optimal treatment; delay in surgery dramatically increases mortality. Incorrect (A): Antibiotics ALONE are completely inadequate for NF - they cannot penetrate necrotic tissue. Immediate surgery is mandatory. Incorrect (C): There is NO time for elective biopsy and culture-directed therapy. NF is a surgical emergency - delay = death. Incorrect (D): Waiting 48 hours for surgical response is unacceptable in NF. Every hour of delay significantly increases mortality. EXAM PEARL: NF type I = polymicrobial (diabetics, immunocompromised) = gas-forming organisms (Clostridium, E. coli, Bacteroides). NF type II = Group A Streptococcus = 'flesh-eating bacteria' = young healthy adults. LRINEC score ≥6 = high suspicion. Hallmark: pain out of proportion to physical findings initially. 'Dishwater' grey fluid at surgery.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A 45-year-old fair-skinned woman presents with persistent centrofacial erythema, visible telangiectasias on the nose and cheeks, and occasional flushing triggered by hot drinks and alcohol. There are no papules or pustules. What is the subtype and MOST appropriate treatment?

options.A: Rosacea subtype 1 (erythematotelangiectatic); oral doxycycline 100mg BD for 3 months
options.B: Rosacea subtype 1 (erythematotelangiectatic); topical brimonidine 0.33% gel (vasoconstrictor) for erythema; laser/IPL for telangiectasias
options.C: Rosacea subtype 2 (papulopustular); topical azelaic acid and oral tetracycline
options.D: Rosacea subtype 3 (phymatous); isotretinoin 0.3mg/kg/day

questions.explanation: Correct (B): This is rosacea subtype 1 (erythematotelangiectatic rosacea - ETR): persistent erythema + telangiectasias + flushing, NO papules/pustules. Management: (1) Topical brimonidine 0.33% gel (α2-adrenergic agonist, vasoconstrictor) = FDA-approved for persistent erythema in ETR - works within 30 minutes, lasts 8-12 hours. (2) Laser/IPL for fixed telangiectasias. (3) Trigger avoidance (heat, spicy food, alcohol, UV). Incorrect (A): Oral doxycycline (40mg modified-release = anti-inflammatory dose, or 100mg) is the treatment for papulopustular rosacea (subtype 2), not purely erythematotelangiectatic rosacea. This patient has NO papules/pustules. Incorrect (C): Subtype 2 = papulopustular (resembles acne but no comedones) = topical metronidazole/azelaic acid/ivermectin + oral doxycycline. Not applicable here. Incorrect (D): Subtype 3 = phymatous rosacea = tissue hypertrophy = rhinophyma = isotretinoin or ablative laser/surgical treatment. EXAM PEARL: Rosacea subtypes: 1=ETR, 2=papulopustular, 3=phymatous, 4=ocular. Ocular rosacea (blepharitis, meibomian gland dysfunction) - treat with oral tetracyclines. Rosacea triggers: sun, heat, exercise, spicy food, alcohol, stress. Demodex folliculorum implicated in pathogenesis.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A 28-year-old woman of Fitzpatrick skin type V presents with dark brown patches on the cheeks and forehead following resolution of acne. Wood's lamp shows accentuation of the patches. What is the first-line treatment for this patient?

options.A: Q-switched Nd:YAG laser 1064nm
options.B: Strict daily photoprotection with SPF 50+ sunscreen + hydroquinone 2-4% cream
options.C: Oral tranexamic acid 500mg twice daily for 3 months
options.D: Medium-depth chemical peel (35% TCA)

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation (PIH) in dark skin types (Fitzpatrick IV-VI) requires careful management. Wood's lamp accentuation = epidermal melanin. First-line = strict sun protection (SPF 50+ daily, physical blockers) + topical hydroquinone 2-4% (tyrosinase inhibitor, bleaching agent) - most evidence-based combination. Incorrect (A): Q-switched Nd:YAG laser is used for resistant hyperpigmentation but carries significant risk of post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation and hypopigmentation in dark skin types - not first-line. Incorrect (C): Oral tranexamic acid (plasminogen inhibitor, reduces melanin transfer) is used for melasma and is increasingly used for PIH, but is not first-line before topical therapy is tried. Incorrect (D): Medium-depth chemical peels (TCA 35%) carry significant risk of worsening PIH in dark skin types and should only be performed by experienced practitioners as adjunctive treatment, not first-line. EXAM PEARL: PIH management ladder: Sunscreen + Hydroquinone → Add tretinoin/AHA → Add azelaic acid/niacinamide/kojic acid → Chemical peel → Laser. Dark skin types have 5x more PIH risk from inflammatory conditions. Hydroquinone >4% = exogenous ochronosis risk (paradoxical darkening) with prolonged use.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A 22-year-old man with dark skin type (Fitzpatrick V) presents with a firm, raised, itchy mass on the chest following a minor injury 8 months ago. The lesion extends beyond the original wound margin and shows no signs of regression. He had a similar keloid excised surgically 2 years ago that recurred within 3 months, even larger. What is the MOST appropriate management to reduce recurrence?

options.A: Simple surgical excision alone with 5mm clear margins
options.B: Surgical excision + intralesional triamcinolone acetonide injections post-operatively + consider adjuvant radiotherapy
options.C: Intralesional 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) injections once weekly for 8 weeks as monotherapy
options.D: Systemic retinoids for 6 months then surgery

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Previous keloid recurrence after surgery indicates high recurrence risk. Best practice for recurrent keloids = Surgery + adjuvant therapy. Post-operative triamcinolone acetonide (intralesional, 10-40mg/mL) starting within days of surgery and continued monthly for 6-12 months significantly reduces recurrence. Adjuvant superficial radiotherapy (8-12Gy within 24-48 hours of surgery) is highly effective for recurrent/large keloids. Incorrect (A): Surgery alone carries 45-100% recurrence rate for keloids, especially in dark skin types and chest location. Simple excision without adjuvant therapy is inadequate given previous recurrence. Incorrect (C): Intralesional 5-FU (antimetabolite) is used for refractory keloids/hypertrophic scars often in combination with triamcinolone (5-FU + TAC combo > monotherapy) but is not the most appropriate when surgery is indicated for a large mass. Incorrect (D): Systemic retinoids have no established role in keloid prevention. EXAM PEARL: Keloid vs Hypertrophic scar: Keloid = extends beyond wound edges + occurs in dark skin + chest/ear/shoulder predilection + doesn't regress spontaneously. Hypertrophic = within wound edges + regresses over months. Keloid treatment ladder: Intralesional TAC → 5-FU+TAC → Pulsed dye laser → Surgery + adjuvant therapy + RT.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A 45-year-old woman presents with intensely itchy, violaceous, polygonal flat-topped papules on the flexor aspects of wrists. Examination of the oral cavity shows a white lacy pattern on the buccal mucosa (Wickham's striae). Nail examination shows pterygium formation of the right thumb nail.
