Which of the following is TRUE about this condition?

options.A: The oral lesions are benign and do not require long-term surveillance
options.B: The disease is caused by IgA-mediated autoimmunity against type VII collagen
options.C: The nail pterygium formation indicates progressive matrix scarring and is irreversible
options.D: First-line treatment for cutaneous LP is oral psoralen + UVA (PUVA)

questions.explanation: Correct (C): Lichen planus of the nail matrix can cause pterygium unguis - the nail plate splits and the proximal nail fold epithelium adheres to the nail bed, resulting in irreversible scarring of the matrix. Early treatment with intralesional or systemic steroids may halt progression but established pterygium is permanent. Incorrect (A): Oral erosive/reticular lichen planus carries a low but real risk of malignant transformation to SCC (estimated 0.5-5% over years). Long-term surveillance is MANDATORY - especially for erosive oral LP. Incorrect (B): LP is mediated by CD8+ T-cell cytotoxic attack against basal keratinocytes with autoimmunity against unknown epidermal antigens. NOT IgA or type VII collagen. (Type VII collagen = EBA and Bullous SLE target). Incorrect (D): First-line for cutaneous LP = topical corticosteroids (potent, e.g., clobetasol propionate). Oral antihistamines for pruritus. PUVA/NB-UVB is used for refractory/widespread LP, not first-line. EXAM PEARL: LP mnemonic: 6 P's = Pruritic, Planar (flat-topped), Purple, Polygonal, Papules, Pattern (Wickham's striae). Histology: Band-like lymphocytic infiltrate at DEJ + sawtooth rete ridges + Civatte bodies (apoptotic keratinocytes). LP associations: Hepatitis C, drugs (beta-blockers, NSAIDs, gold, antimalarials = lichenoid drug eruption).

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A 45-year-old obese diabetic man presents with brown-red, well-demarcated, slightly scaly patches in the groin and axillae for 3 months. Wood's lamp examination of the affected skin shows coral-red fluorescence. KOH examination is negative. What is the causative organism and treatment?

options.A: Trichophyton rubrum; oral terbinafine for 2 weeks
options.B: Corynebacterium minutissimum; oral erythromycin or topical clindamycin/fusidic acid
options.C: Malassezia furfur; oral itraconazole for 7 days
options.D: Staphylococcus aureus; oral flucloxacillin

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Erythrasma is caused by Corynebacterium minutissimum (gram-positive bacterium), NOT a fungus. Characteristic coral-red fluorescence under Wood's lamp is due to porphyrins produced by the bacteria. KOH negative (confirms non-fungal). Predisposing factors: obesity, diabetes, hyperhidrosis, tropical climate, immunosuppression. Treatment: oral erythromycin 250mg QID for 14 days OR topical antibiotics (clindamycin, fusidic acid, mupirocin). Incorrect (A): Trichophyton causes tinea cruris - KOH would show fungal hyphae, Wood's lamp shows no coral-red fluorescence. Treatment with antifungals. Incorrect (C): Malassezia causes tinea versicolor - 'spaghetti and meatballs' on KOH, yellow-green Wood's lamp fluorescence (inconsistent). Groin is not typical site. Incorrect (D): Staphylococcus causes impetigo, folliculitis, cellulitis - not brown-red scaly intertriginous patches with coral-red fluorescence. EXAM PEARL: Coral-red fluorescence = ERYTHRASMA (Corynebacterium) = BACTERIAL. Green fluorescence = Pseudomonas. Bright green = Microsporum (fungal). Blue-white = Vitiligo. Orange-yellow = Tinea versicolor (inconsistent). Erythrasma vs Tinea cruris: Erythrasma = no active border, no central clearing, coral-red fluorescence, KOH negative.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A 30-year-old man presents with intensely itchy grouped vesicles and papules symmetrically distributed over elbows, knees, and buttocks. He also reports bloating and loose stools. Small bowel biopsy shows subtotal villous atrophy. Direct immunofluorescence of perilesional skin shows granular IgA at the tips of dermal papillae. What is the management?

options.A: Oral steroids (prednisolone 1mg/kg/day) and gluten-free diet
options.B: Dapsone 100mg/day (for immediate symptom control) + strict lifelong gluten-free diet
options.C: Rituximab (anti-CD20) and dietary modification
options.D: Colchicine and topical clobetasol

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Dermatitis Herpetiformis (DH) is the cutaneous manifestation of coeliac disease (gluten-sensitive enteropathy). DIF showing granular IgA at dermal papillae tips = pathognomonic. Management has two components: (1) Dapsone = immediate rapid relief of pruritus and blistering (inhibits neutrophil function) - does NOT treat the underlying bowel disease. (2) Lifelong strict gluten-free diet = treats both the bowel disease AND the skin disease (dapsone can often be tapered/stopped after years of GFD). Incorrect (A): Systemic steroids have NO established role in DH. GFD is essential but dapsone is the immediate treatment. Incorrect (C): Rituximab (B-cell depleting agent) is used for pemphigus/BP - no role in DH. Incorrect (D): Colchicine has limited evidence as second-line if dapsone intolerant. Topical clobetasol alone cannot control DH. EXAM PEARL: DH associations: Coeliac disease (100%), thyroid disease, IgA nephropathy (same IgA deposits). Anti-tTG IgA + anti-endomysial IgA positive. Dapsone side effects: haemolytic anaemia (G6PD screen before use), methemoglobinaemia, agranulocytosis, peripheral neuropathy. Check G6PD before dapsone. Long-term GFD reduces risk of GI lymphoma.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A 4-month-old girl presents with a rapidly growing, bright red, raised vascular lesion over the right upper eyelid and nose that appeared at 3 weeks of age. It is now causing ptosis and obscuring the visual axis. The parents are told it usually resolves by age 7-10 years. What is the MOST appropriate treatment at this time?

options.A: Watchful waiting as spontaneous involution is guaranteed
options.B: Oral propranolol 1-3mg/kg/day (or topical timolol 0.5% gel for small lesions)
options.C: Intralesional triamcinolone acetonide injection only
options.D: Pulsed dye laser (PDL) immediately

questions.explanation: Correct (B): This is a large, segmental infantile hemangioma (IH) in a vision-threatening location - the lesion is covering the visual axis and causing ptosis, risking amblyopia (functional blindness from deprivation). This is an absolute indication for treatment. Oral propranolol (non-selective beta-blocker) is the FIRST-LINE treatment for complicated IH since 2014 FDA approval. It causes rapid vasoconstriction, reduces proliferation, and promotes apoptosis. Topical timolol 0.5% (beta-blocker gel) is effective for small/superficial IH. Incorrect (A): Watchful waiting is appropriate for small, uncomplicated IH not causing functional compromise or ulceration. In this case with visual axis obstruction + ptosis, waiting risks permanent amblyopia in the critical visual development period (first years of life). Incorrect (C): Intralesional triamcinolone was the pre-propranolol treatment for periorbital IH but is now second-line due to rare risk of retinal artery embolism when injected around the eye. Not first-line for large lesions. Incorrect (D): PDL targets superficial vessels; it does NOT reduce the bulk of a large proliferating IH and is more useful post-involution for residual telangiectasias. EXAM PEARL: IH = most common benign tumor of infancy. Appears at 3-4 weeks, proliferates to age 9-12 months, then involutes. PHACES syndrome = large facial segmental IH + Posterior fossa anomalies, Hemangiomas, Arterial anomalies, Cardiac defects, Eye anomalies, Sternal clefting. Indications for treatment: vision/airway compromise, ulceration, large facial/functionally-significant lesions.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A 20-year-old woman presents with an oval, scaly patch on the trunk followed 2 weeks later by multiple smaller similar lesions arranged in a 'Christmas tree' pattern along Langer's lines on her back. She had a mild upper respiratory illness 2 weeks before the first patch appeared. Which is TRUE about this condition?

options.A: It is caused by dermatophyte fungi and requires oral antifungal therapy
options.B: It is associated with HHV-6 and HHV-7 reactivation; 'herald patch' appears first; it is self-limiting in 6-8 weeks
options.C: It requires skin biopsy to confirm diagnosis before treatment
options.D: It is a manifestation of secondary syphilis and requires penicillin treatment

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Pityriasis rosea (PR) - classic presentation: Herald patch (first, large, oval, scaly) → 2 weeks later generalized eruption in Christmas tree pattern along skin cleavage lines. Associated with HHV-6 and HHV-7 reactivation (strong evidence). Self-limiting in 6-8 weeks typically (some cases up to 12 weeks). Treatment: reassurance, emollients, antihistamines for itch. Oral acyclovir/erythromycin may slightly reduce duration. Incorrect (A): PR is viral, NOT fungal. KOH is negative. Antifungals have no benefit. Incorrect (C): Diagnosis is clinical. Biopsy is NOT routinely needed unless diagnosis is uncertain (particularly to exclude secondary syphilis or parapsoriasis). Incorrect (D): This is the important differential - secondary syphilis can mimic PR (oval scaly lesions). However, syphilitic lesions affect palms and soles (rare in PR), herald patch is absent, and RPR/VDRL will be positive. PR is viral, not syphilitic. EXAM PEARL: PR differential: Secondary syphilis (check RPR/VDRL especially if palm/sole involvement or atypical features), guttate psoriasis, tinea corporis. Drug-induced PR-like eruption: gold, captopril, barbiturates, bismuth. PR in pregnancy = associated with fetal loss if early onset (<15 weeks).

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A 30-year-old MSM presents with a tender inguinal mass with a 'groove sign' (linear depression between two groups of enlarged nodes divided by Poupart's ligament). He recalls a small self-healing genital papule 3 weeks ago. Frei test is reported as positive. What is the diagnosis and treatment?

options.A: Chancroid (H. ducreyi); azithromycin 1g single dose
options.B: Lymphogranuloma Venereum (Chlamydia trachomatis L1-L3); doxycycline 100mg BD for 21 days
options.C: Donovanosis (K. granulomatis); doxycycline 100mg BD for 3 weeks
options.D: Bubonic plague (Yersinia pestis); streptomycin or gentamicin

questions.explanation: Correct (B): LGV (Lymphogranuloma Venereum) - caused by Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1, L2, L3 (invasive strains, unlike D-K causing NGU). Classic stages: Primary (small, self-healing papule/ulcer) → Secondary (painful inguinal lymphadenopathy + groove sign in 20% + bubo formation) → Tertiary (genital elephantiasis, rectal strictures - 'esthiomène'). Groove sign = pathognomonic of LGV. Treatment: Doxycycline 100mg BD for 21 days (not 7 days as for non-LGV chlamydia). Frei test (intradermal killed chlamydia antigen - positive in LGV) is now obsolete/not used widely but positive result mentioned. Incorrect (A): Chancroid (H. ducreyi) causes a painful ulcer + bubo, but groove sign is NOT a feature. Treatment = azithromycin or ciprofloxacin (shorter course). Incorrect (C): Donovanosis does NOT cause significant lymphadenopathy (pseudobuboes are subcutaneous granulomas, not true LN enlargement). Groove sign absent. Progressive painless genital ulceration is the hallmark. Incorrect (D): Plague (Yersinia) = zoonotic (rodent/flea bite), fever + systemic illness + extreme toxicity. Not an STI in the context of MSM/sexual exposure. EXAM PEARL: LGV stages: Primary (ulcer, often missed) → Secondary (bubo, groove sign) → Tertiary (elephantiasis, rectal strictures). Increased in MSM (anorectal LGV). Treatment: Doxycycline 21 days OR Erythromycin 21 days (pregnancy). Aspirate buboes; do NOT incise (sinus tract formation).

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A 30-year-old obese woman with BMI 38 presents with recurrent painful nodules, abscesses, and sinus tracts in the bilateral axillae and groin for 5 years. Multiple courses of antibiotics have given only partial and temporary relief. She has Hurley Stage III disease. She is a smoker. Examination shows interconnected sinus tracts and significant scarring. Which is the MOST appropriate biologic treatment?

options.A: Secukinumab (anti-IL-17A) 300mg SC weekly for 5 doses then monthly
options.B: Adalimumab (anti-TNF) 160mg at week 0, 80mg at week 2, then 40mg weekly
options.C: Dupilumab (anti-IL-4/13) 300mg SC every 2 weeks
options.D: Ustekinumab (anti-IL12/23) 45mg SC at 0, 4 weeks, then every 12 weeks

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Adalimumab is the ONLY FDA/EMA-approved biologic for Hidradenitis Suppurativa (HS). The approved dosing regimen is: 160mg at week 0 → 80mg at week 2 → 40mg weekly from week 4. Based on PIONEER I and II trials showing significant reduction in abscess and inflammatory nodule count. Hurley Stage III (extensive scarring, sinus tracts) with refractory disease = clear indication for biologic therapy. Incorrect (A): Secukinumab (anti-IL-17A, approved for psoriasis, PsA, ankylosing spondylitis) has Phase 2 evidence for HS but is NOT currently FDA-approved for HS. Not the most appropriate approved option. Incorrect (C): Dupilumab is approved for atopic dermatitis, not HS. IL-4/13 pathway is not the primary target in HS pathogenesis. Incorrect (D): Ustekinumab (approved for psoriasis, PsA, Crohn's, UC) has some case reports in HS but is NOT approved for HS. EXAM PEARL: HS pathogenesis: follicular occlusion → rupture → secondary infection → chronic inflammation (TNF, IL-1β, IL-6, IL-17 driven). Risk factors: obesity, smoking, hormonal factors. Hurley staging: I (nodules/abscesses, no sinuses) → II (sinuses, moderate) → III (extensive sinuses, widespread scarring). Isotretinoin is largely ineffective for HS. Weight loss and smoking cessation are essential.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A 35-year-old immunocompromised (HIV, CD4 120) man presents with hundreds of umbilicated, pearly, dome-shaped papules distributed widely on the face, trunk, and genitalia. Some lesions are very large (giant molluscum, >1cm). What is the MOST appropriate management strategy?

options.A: Topical imiquimod 5% cream to all lesions three times weekly
options.B: Optimize ART (antiretroviral therapy) to improve immune function; treat individual lesions with cryotherapy/curettage; topical cidofovir for extensive disease
options.C: Oral valacyclovir 1g TID for 2 weeks
options.D: Observation only as molluscum is self-limiting

questions.explanation: Correct (B): In HIV-associated extensive molluscum contagiosum, the underlying immunosuppression (low CD4) is the primary problem. Management approach: (1) Optimize ART - immune reconstitution (CD4 recovery) is the most important step - lesions often resolve spontaneously with immune recovery. (2) Physical destruction of individual lesions (cryotherapy, curettage, or laser) for cosmetically significant ones. (3) Topical cidofovir 1-3% cream has evidence for extensive/giant molluscum in immunocompromised patients. Incorrect (A): Imiquimod (immune response modifier) requires functioning cellular immunity to work - in severely immunocompromised patients (CD4 120), imiquimod is unlikely to be effective as it needs CD4 T-cells to mount immune response. Incorrect (C): Molluscum is caused by Molluscum Contagiosum Virus (MCV - poxvirus), NOT herpesvirus. Valacyclovir (anti-herpes) has no antiviral activity against MCV. Incorrect (D): Molluscum in HIV with CD4 120 will NOT self-limit - it will continue to spread extensively. Immune reconstitution through ART is needed. EXAM PEARL: MC in immunocompetent = self-limiting (6-24 months); in HIV = marker of advanced disease, won't resolve without immune recovery. Giant molluscum >5mm = characteristic of severe immunosuppression. MCV is not culturable in routine labs. Giant/extensive facial MC in an adult = consider HIV testing.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A 55-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes presents with a slowly expanding, irregularly shaped, yellow-brown atrophic plaque with a violaceous border on the anterior shin. The center has multiple telangiectasias. No pain is reported. A previous biopsy showed palisading granulomas with necrobiosis of collagen in the dermis and a surrounding plasma cell/histiocytic infiltrate. What is the diagnosis and the MOST accurate statement about this condition?

options.A: Granuloma annulare; treatment with topical steroids is curative
options.B: Necrobiosis Lipoidica (NL); 65-75% of patients have diabetes, but NL can also occur without diabetes; ulceration occurs in 35% and is a major complication
options.C: Pretibial myxedema; indicates hypothyroidism and responds to levothyroxine
options.D: Acanthosis nigricans of the shin; indicates severe insulin resistance

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Necrobiosis Lipoidica (Diabeticorum): classic yellow-brown atrophic plaques with violaceous border + telangiectasias on pretibial areas. Histology shows palisading granulomas with full-thickness dermal necrobiosis (collagen degeneration) + plasma cells + histiocytes. Important facts: 65-75% of NL patients have DM, but only 0.3% of diabetics develop NL. NL can occur in non-diabetics. Ulceration in 35% is a major complication (trauma, venous stasis). Treatment: potent topical steroids, intralesional steroids, tacrolimus. No perfect treatment. Incorrect (A): Granuloma annulare - ring-shaped papules, often on dorsal hands, typically in young adults. Histology shows palisading granulomas but WITHOUT plasma cell infiltrate and necrobiosis is more focal. Generally resolves spontaneously. NOT on shins with yellow-brown atrophic center. Incorrect (C): Pretibial myxedema = non-pitting waxy/indurated skin on shins associated with HYPERTHYROIDISM (Graves' disease), not hypothyroidism. Mucinous deposits - different histology. Incorrect (D): Acanthosis nigricans = velvety, hyperpigmented plaques in body folds (neck, axillae, groin) - NOT atrophic plaques with telangiectasias on shins. EXAM PEARL: NL + Granuloma Annulare + Sarcoidosis = 'necrobiotic granulomas'. NL ulceration treatment = wound care + pentoxifylline + TNF inhibitors. NL does NOT regress with improved diabetes control.
